title: 2 Samuel 14:21–33
context: David permits Absalom’s return but refuses to see him, and Absalom lives two years in Jerusalem estranged from his father. The narrator describes Absalom’s striking appearance and his family, including a daughter named Tamar. When Joab ignores him, Absalom burns Joab’s field to force a meeting, demands to see the king, and receives a kiss. The reconciliation is outward only, without repentance or justice, and leads into Absalom’s rebellion. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the costs of unresolved sin.

verses.text: The king said to Joab, “Behold now, I have granted this thing. Go therefore, and bring the young man Absalom back.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king tells Joab that he grants the request and orders him to bring back the young man Absalom. Joab’s scheme succeeds.

Arminian readers see David yielding to persuasion and his own longing.
verses.reformedNotes:
David agrees to Absalom’s return. The decision is made without addressing Amnon’s murder.

Reformed readers see a reconciliation begun without justice or repentance. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the return will prove incomplete and costly.

verses.text: Joab fell to the ground on his face, showed respect, and blessed the king. Joab said, “Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord, O king, in that the king has performed the request of his servant.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab bows and blesses the king, saying he knows he has found favor because the king granted his request. He is pleased.

Arminian readers see Joab’s success strengthening his position at court.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joab treats the decision as a sign of royal favor toward himself. His interests are served.

Reformed readers see mixed motives in court politics. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without speculating beyond the text about Joab’s deeper aims.

verses.text: So Joab arose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab goes to Geshur and brings Absalom to Jerusalem. The exile ends.

Arminian readers see a father’s longing fulfilled at least outwardly. Absalom is home, but nothing has yet been said about his crime or about reconciliation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom returns after three years. The action is swift.

Reformed readers see a homecoming that does not yet resolve the deeper breach. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the narrative immediately qualifies the reconciliation in the next verse.

verses.text: The king said, “Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face.” So Absalom returned to his own house, and didn’t see the king’s face.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king says Absalom may return to his house but must not see his face. Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing the king.

Arminian readers see a half-measure that leaves the relationship broken.
verses.reformedNotes:
David allows return without restoration. The arrangement satisfies neither justice nor reconciliation.

Reformed readers see the instability of a compromise that avoids the real issue. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the tension it creates in the following verses.

verses.text: Now in all Israel there was no one to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty. From the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no defect in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
No one in Israel is praised as much as Absalom for his beauty; he has no defect from head to foot. His appearance is striking.

Arminian readers note that outward appeal can mask inner danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
The description recalls Saul’s impressive appearance (1 Samuel 9:2) and God’s warning that he looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

Reformed readers see a caution against judging by appearance. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without treating Absalom’s looks as a moral verdict in themselves.

verses.text: When he cut the hair of his head (now it was at every year’s end that he cut it; because it was heavy on him, therefore he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels, after the king’s weight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom cuts his hair yearly because it is heavy, and it weighs two hundred shekels by the royal weight. This is about two kilograms or 4.4 pounds.

Arminian readers see a detail emphasizing Absalom’s striking image.
verses.reformedNotes:
The hair detail may anticipate his death in 18:9, though the text there mentions his head rather than his hair.

Reformed readers likewise hold the connection lightly. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without building more on the detail than it supports.

verses.text: Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman with a beautiful face.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom has three sons and a daughter named Tamar, a beautiful woman. The name recalls his sister.

Arminian readers see a tender detail, perhaps honoring the sister whose wrong he resented.
verses.reformedNotes:
Naming his daughter Tamar may reflect his love for his sister, though the text does not say. 18:18 later suggests Absalom had no surviving son.

Reformed readers hold these details carefully. Both traditions read this as shared ground and remember Tamar’s desolation in 13:20.

verses.text: Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, and he didn’t see the king’s face.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom lives two full years in Jerusalem without seeing the king’s face. The estrangement continues.

Arminian readers see the cost of reconciliation left incomplete. Nearness without relationship breeds frustration on both sides.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two more years pass. The partial return has not healed the breach.

Reformed readers see how unresolved wrong festers. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the delay will push Absalom toward forceful action, as the next verses show.

verses.text: Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he would not come to him. Then he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom sends for Joab to go to the king, but Joab refuses twice. Absalom is ignored.

Arminian readers see Joab now keeping his distance, perhaps cautious about further involvement in the royal family’s quarrel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joab declines without explanation. Absalom’s frustration grows.

Reformed readers see court tensions unresolved. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without speculating beyond the text about Joab’s reasons for refusing to come to Absalom.

verses.text: Therefore he said to his servants, “Behold, Joab’s field is near mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom tells his servants to set Joab’s barley field on fire, and they do. He forces Joab’s attention.

Arminian readers see Absalom’s willingness to use destructive means to get his way.
verses.reformedNotes:
The burning of the field shows Absalom’s ruthlessness. It foreshadows his later actions.

Reformed readers see a pattern of violence and manipulation. Both traditions read this with moral clarity and as shared ground, recognizing the character that will emerge in Absalom’s rebellion.

verses.text: Then Joab arose and came to Absalom to his house, and said to him, “Why have your servants set my field on fire?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab comes to Absalom’s house and asks why his servants set his field on fire. The tactic works.

Arminian readers see Absalom achieving his goal through coercion. Pressure, not persuasion, brings Joab to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joab responds to force, not request. The confrontation brings him to Absalom.

Reformed readers see how coercion can succeed in the short term. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting that the means used do not reflect justice or reconciliation.

verses.text: Absalom answered Joab, “Behold, I sent to you, saying, ‘Come here, that I may send you to the king, to say, “Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore, let me see the king’s face; and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom says he wanted Joab to ask the king why he returned from Geshur; he demands to see the king, and if he is guilty, let the king kill him. He presses the issue.

Arminian readers see defiance rather than repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom challenges the king to judge him or receive him. He does not confess his crime.

Reformed readers see a demand for restoration without contrition. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that Absalom’s words differ from genuine repentance.

verses.text: So Joab came to the king and told him; and when he had called for Absalom, he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king; and the king kissed Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab tells the king, Absalom comes and bows to the ground, and the king kisses him. Outward reconciliation occurs.

Arminian readers see a moment of restoration that lacks repentance and justice, and so remains incomplete.
verses.reformedNotes:
The kiss signals acceptance, but no words of confession or forgiveness are recorded. Chapter 15 follows with Absalom’s rebellion.

Reformed readers see a reconciliation that heals nothing beneath the surface. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the costs of unaddressed sin.
